sections.html:
Both offices are in Tucson. The Pima County Assessor values and classifies property, takes appeals and runs the valuation relief programs. The Pima County Treasurer mails statements, collects payments and sells tax liens on delinquent accounts. Because the Treasurer can't change a bill unless the Board of Supervisors directs it, a dispute over value starts with the Assessor.

  • Treasurer: 240 N. Stone Avenue, lower level of the Pima County Public Service Center, Tucson, AZ 85701. Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., (520) 724-8341.
  • Assessor: 240 N Stone Ave, Tucson, AZ 85701, (520) 724-8630. The Valuation Relief team is at (520) 724-7500.

The first half is due October 1 and the second half March 1. Each becomes delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on the following November 1 or May 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052). Statements go out in mid-September, and that is the only one you receive unless the account turns delinquent. Delinquent real property notices go out in August and January.

For tax year 2026, the Treasurer's calendar lists December 31, 2026 as the full-year payment date. The second half is due March 1, 2027, with a postmark deadline of May 3, 2027 because May 1 is a Saturday. No interest is collected on a full-year payment made by December 31 of the tax year (A.R.S. 42-18053), so an open bill can still be settled in full before year-end.

sections.h2: Delinquent taxes and the lien sale
sections.html:
Interest runs at 16 percent a year, simple, from delinquency, and part of a month counts as a whole one. Tax unpaid before January of the next year picks up another $5.00 or 5 percent penalty. In February the delinquent lien goes to the Treasurer's tax lien sale, held in the last week of the month. No bidding happens on Tuesday, since the Board of Supervisors meets that day.

The buyer purchases the lien on your taxes. Three years after the sale date, that buyer may foreclose and acquire the property. If you are thinking of selling, these details matter.

  • Once a lien is sold, the Treasurer can't take partial payments. All delinquent taxes, interest, penalties and fees must be paid together.
  • Before a sale, the minimum payment covers the tax, interest and fees for one delinquent installment, meaning a half-year.
  • State law allows one lien to cover all the delinquent taxes on a parcel, not just one year (A.R.S. 42-18104).

Pay online, by mail or in person. Online payment uses ACH or electronic check, with a minimum payment of the greater of $10 or 10 percent of the installment due. The online convenience fee goes entirely to the payment servicer.

  • Mail: send the coupon with a check, cashier's check or money order in US funds to PO Box 29011, Phoenix, AZ 85038-9011. Write your state code or reference number on the check, and never mail cash.
  • In person: cash, check or card at the Treasurer's counter. Credit and debit cards carry a 2 percent service fee.
  • Wire: call (520) 724-8341 first.

Mortgage and tax service companies can get tax statement information on request, so a lender that escrows your taxes should already have the bill. Liability covers the calendar year, January through December, even though the second installment falls due in the following year.

Multiply limited value by the assessment ratio and the combined tax rate, then divide by $100. Primary and secondary taxes are figured the same way and added. Primary tax pays a jurisdiction's operating expenses and applies to the limited cash value. Secondary tax pays for special districts such as fire districts, and for voter-approved bonds and budget overrides.

Your rate combines every jurisdiction that taxes your address, such as the City of Tucson, Pima County and your school district. Two bill items are worth knowing.

  • Primary Tax Reduction: a credit on the school district's primary levy for owner-occupied homes, sometimes called the homeowner's rebate. The state reimburses the school district for eligible amounts.
  • Fire District Assistance: a countywide tax on every taxable property that supplements fire districts, levied under A.R.S. 48-807.

The Assessor has no say over levies or rates. If you think your rate is too high, contact the political subdivisions listed on your bill.

Petition the Assessor within 60 days after the mail date of the Notice of Value (A.R.S. 42-16051). Notices of Value go out on or before March 1, and a Notice of Change mailed on or before September 30 has its own supplemental appeal. An assessment appeal tries to show that the property was valued improperly, given the wrong class, or assigned an incorrect limited value. It isn't a complaint about higher taxes.

The petition must state a valuation method with supporting data.

  • Market approach: include the sale price of at least one comparable property in the same area, or the sale of your own property.
  • Replacement cost approach: include the cost to build or rebuild plus the land value.
  • Income approach: include the information A.R.S. 42-16052 requires.

A Notice of Claim covers a factual error, and a Notice of Proposed Correction can arrive by certified mail at any time of year. Pay the tax as billed while an appeal is pending. If a correction lowers the tax, you get the overpayment back with interest at the rate set by the Arizona Department of Revenue. If it raises the tax, you have 60 days to pay the increase without interest.

Valuation Relief programs lower or freeze the limited assessed value for qualifying owners, each under strict statutory eligibility rules for the applicant and household. The yearly filing deadline is March 1, and later applications must include a Redemption Waiver form under A.R.S. 42-11153.

The Assessor currently features the exemption for a veteran with a 100 percent service-connected disability. H.B. 2792, signed February 12, 2026, clarified A.R.S. 42-11111 as an emergency measure effective for tax year 2026 and after. The veteran must be honorably discharged, hold a VA benefit summary letter confirming the 100 percent rating and meet the income limit. One primary residence qualifies. Call (520) 724-7500 or write ASRValRelief@pima.gov for current forms.

Pima County is home to an estimated 1,074,685 people, and 65.2 percent of housing units are owner-occupied. If you sell with tax still open, ask the title company for a payoff that includes interest through closing, and ask the Treasurer whether a lien has already been sold on the parcel. A sold lien changes what you must pay, since partial payments are no longer accepted.

Steps that help: look up your parcel and see which installments are open, request the payoff dated to closing, send it to title, and check that the settlement statement matches. A cash buyer can close quickly, which limits how much interest builds, but all delinquent taxes, interest, penalties and fees still come out of your proceeds.

faqs.q: When are Pima County property taxes due?
faqs.a: October 1 for the first half and March 1 for the second, delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1. For 2026, the full year is due December 31, 2026, and second-half payments need a postmark by May 3, 2027.

faqs.q: What interest does Pima County charge on late taxes?
faqs.a: Sixteen percent a year, simple, from the delinquency date, with a partial month counted whole. Taxes unpaid into January add $5.00 or 5 percent. A full-year payment by December 31 carries no interest.

faqs.q: What is the Pima County tax lien sale?
faqs.a: The Treasurer sells the lien for delinquent taxes in the last week of February. You keep the house until the lien buyer forecloses, which can happen after three years from the sale date.

faqs.q: Can I pay Pima County property tax online?
faqs.a: Yes, by ACH or electronic check, with a minimum of the greater of $10 or 10 percent of the installment. You can also mail a check to PO Box 29011, Phoenix, AZ 85038-9011, or pay at 240 N. Stone Avenue in Tucson.

faqs.q: Who do I call if my Pima County valuation looks wrong?
faqs.a: The Assessor, at (520) 724-8630. The Treasurer can't change a bill unless the Board of Supervisors directs it. File within 60 days of the Notice of Value mail date, and keep paying the bill as issued during the appeal.
